packages.oneLiner: Command-line client for FlutterFlow to export code and build apps with AI.

explainer.whatItDoes: The FlutterFlow CLI allows developers to export code from FlutterFlow projects, deploy Firebase configurations, and use FlutterFlow AI to build and edit applications declaratively from the terminal using an MCP server for coding agents.
useWhen: You want to export your FlutterFlow project code directly into your local editor.
You want coding agents like Claude Code or Cursor to build and edit your FlutterFlow app declaratively.
You need to deploy your FlutterFlow project's Firebase configuration from the command line.
avoidWhen: You are building a standard Flutter app without using FlutterFlow.
You need a general-purpose local state management or utility library for standard Flutter apps.
strengths: Direct integration with FlutterFlow projects and export workflows.
Built-in AI workspace support with MCP server integration for assistants like Claude Code and Cursor.
weaknesses: Requires a FlutterFlow account and API token.
Subject to strict licensing constraints under the Business Source License 1.1.
explainer.setupNotes: Activate globally using `dart pub global activate flutterflow_cli` and set your `FLUTTERFLOW_API_TOKEN` environment variable.
explainer.example:
dart pub global activate flutterflow_cli
export FLUTTERFLOW_API_TOKEN=<your token>
flutterflow export-code --project <project id> --dest <output folder>

explainer.whatItDoes: Allows Flutter apps to make HTTP requests using a Rust backend through FFI. It provides support for HTTP/1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3, TLS 1.2/1.3, connection pooling, interceptors, and compatibility with standard dart:io, http, and dio APIs.
useWhen: You need high-performance HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 support across Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux
You want a unified API for HTTP requests that also supports Windows and Linux
You need advanced networking features like certificate pinning, custom DNS resolution, and connection pooling
avoidWhen: You are building for the web platform, which is currently not supported

strengths: Supports HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with reliable performance powered by Rust's reqwest crate
Cross-platform support including desktop operating systems like Windows and Linux
Compatible with existing http and dio client patterns
weaknesses: Requires Rust toolchain installed and increases APK/app size
Web platform is not supported
explainer.setupNotes: Requires installing Rust via rustup (1.80.0 or later), Android NDK / Command-line tools, and calling Rhttp.init() during app start.

packages.name: hit
packages.description: Decouple Flutter layout size from hit-test size, and deliver taps outside parent bounds.
packages.oneLiner: Decouple Flutter layout size from hit-test size to deliver taps outside parent bounds.

explainer.whatItDoes: Separates paint and layout size from hit size in Flutter, allowing widgets to stay visually small while having a larger tap target. Delivers pointer events that fall outside a widget's layout box using a higher-level scope.
useWhen: You need a control to stay visually small like an icon or 1px edge but meet a comfortable touch target size.
You need to handle taps on elements that overflow their parent bounds without breaking neighboring layouts.
avoidWhen: You have hundreds of deferred targets nested under one huge root scope, which can impact performance.
Standard padding or sizing solutions are sufficient and do not cause layout crowding.
strengths: Enables precise separation of paint/layout bounds from hit-test bounds.
Includes a built-in Dart DevTools extension for inspecting hit scopes and debugging missed taps.
Supports slivers via SliverHitScope for custom scroll views.
weaknesses: Deferred hit-testing is O(n) over registered targets on a scope, meaning large numbers of targets can affect performance.
Requires careful scope placement so that the HitScope's layout box actually covers the expanded hit area.
explainer.setupNotes: not documented
explainer.example:
HitScope(
  child: Padding(
    padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
    child: HitLayer(
      alignment: Alignment.center,
      behavior: HitTestBehavior.deferToChild,
      hitChild: GestureDetector(
        behavior: HitTestBehavior.opaque,
        onTap: () {},
        child: const SizedBox(width: 48, height: 48),
      ),
      paintChild: const IgnorePointer(
        child: Icon(Icons.add, size: 24),
      ),
    ),
  ),
)

packages.oneLiner: Animates its child widget to a new position automatically when its position changes requiring no calculation.

explainer.whatItDoes: AnimatedTo tracks its child widget using a GlobalKey and automatically animates the child to its new position whenever a rebuild or layout update shifts it. It supports both curve-based animations and spring physics simulations, alongside features like delayed start and coordinate boundaries for gesture handling.
useWhen: You want to animate a widget smoothly to a new position when reordered or repositioned via state changes.
You need spring physics or curve-based positional animations without manually calculating delta offsets.
You want to create staggered wave-like layout animations easily using the delay parameter.
avoidWhen: You need animations across Sliver-related widgets like ListView where the animation happens across slivers.
You need general non-positional implicit animations or Lottie/Rive animations.
strengths: Requires zero position calculation from the developer.
Supports both curve durations and natural physical spring simulations.
Provides AnimatedToBoundary to correctly handle hit testing and coordinate systems during movement.
weaknesses: Does not work across Sliver-related widgets when the animation happens across slivers.
Requires a GlobalKey to keep the RenderObject alive across depth or position changes.

alternatives.name: flutter_animate
alternatives.why_pick_it: Choose flutter_animate if you prefer a comprehensive chained animation extension library for fading, scaling, and moving widgets.

explainer.example:
AnimatedTo.curve(
  globalKey: _globalKey,
  child: Container(
    width: 60,
    height: 60,
    color: Colors.blue,
  ),
)

useWhen: You need a hierarchical or tree-structured table data view with expandable rows and columns.
You need fixed headers and a fixed first column alongside vertical and horizontal scrolling.
avoidWhen: You only need a standard, flat grid or data table without expandable nested rows and columns.
You require complex chart visualisations rather than tabular text/widget cells.
strengths: Supports nested rows and columns grouped in expandable structures.
Fixed header and first column with vertical and horizontal scrolling.
External controller support for dynamically managing rows and columns.
weaknesses: Limited to table layouts with expandable rows and columns.
Not documented for database ORM or state management patterns beyond basic controller management.

explainer.whatItDoes: Displays a checklist and progress bar under any TextField that update on every keystroke to show which password rules are met or unmet. It supports Unicode characters, custom rules, NIST policies, password generation, and form validation.
useWhen: You need live visual feedback for password creation requirements in a sign-up or change-password form.
You want to share the exact same password policy validation logic between your Flutter frontend and Dart backend.
avoidWhen: You only need standard form validation without real-time checklist and progress UI elements.
strengths: Unicode-aware counting for multi-script, emoji, and accented passwords.
Shareable password rules package with backend support.
Extensively customizable UI, animations, strength labels, and custom item builders.
weaknesses: Limited to password validation and checklist UI use cases.
explainer.example:
FlutterPwValidator(
  controller: controller,
  rules: const PasswordRules(
    minLength: 8,
    uppercase: 1,
    lowercase: 1,
    digits: 1,
    special: 1,
  ),
  onSuccess: () => setState(() => canSubmit = true),
  onFail: () => setState(() => canSubmit = false),
)

weaknesses: Relies on the external simple_animations package.

useWhen: You want clear separation of concerns between UI and logic
You need efficient rebuilds with minimal boilerplate
You prefer a declarative UI approach with testable business logic
avoidWhen: You are already using another state‑management solution like Riverpod or Bloc
You need advanced dependency injection or navigation features not covered by Elementary
strengths: Clear layer separation

Easy to test business logic
weaknesses: Limited to MVVM; no built‑in navigation or DI
Requires learning its specific widget and model classes

explainer.whatItDoes: Nes UI provides a complete set of retro-styled widgets like buttons, checkboxes, containers, and dialogs. It includes a custom ThemeData and integrates with Google Fonts to deliver an 8-bit video game aesthetic.
useWhen: You are building a game UI or a retro-themed application in Flutter.
You want custom pixel-art styled widgets like NesButton, NesContainer, and NesConfirmDialog.
avoidWhen: You require standard Material or Cupertino look and feel.
You want a heavy focus on animations or physics-based motion without retro styling.
strengths: Distinct retro video game aesthetic out of the box.
Custom widgets designed specifically for retro game layouts and menus.
weaknesses: Limited to a very specific retro visual style.
Font loading via Google Fonts requires internet access at runtime unless bundled manually.
explainer.setupNotes: Call WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized() at the main method and add the flutterNesTheme() to your MaterialApp.

packages.oneLiner: Production-focused Flutter utilities for notifications, storage, connectivity, and media.

explainer.whatItDoes: A comprehensive utility package providing pre-configured services for push and local notifications, secure storage, Hive CE, connectivity checking, validation, and media/file pickers. It bundles common everyday extensions and helpers for production apps.
useWhen: You are building a production Flutter app and want a pre-packaged set of utilities for notifications, storage, and common validations.
You need an integrated solution for push/local notifications with deep-link handling and per-category mute preferences.
avoidWhen: You only need a single lightweight utility (like url_launcher or crypto) and want to avoid pulling in a large dependency graph.
Your project does not use Flutter 3.47+ or Dart 3.13+.
strengths: Combines many essential production utilities into a single, cohesive package.
Built-in support for per-category notification mute, cold-start taps, and in-app notification overlays.
Type-safe Result and AsyncState types for robust error handling.
weaknesses: Large dependency footprint due to covering multiple domains (storage, media, notifications, location).
Strict minimum requirement of Flutter 3.47 and Dart 3.13.
explainer.setupNotes: Requires initialisation in main() before runApp and specific platform configurations for Firebase, permissions, and minimum SDK versions (Android minSdk 24, compileSdk 37).
